intro: The third part of section 34.4 turns to Erik H. Erikson, who carried psychoanalysis beyond childhood into the whole life cycle. It follows his life from art student and Vienna schoolteacher to child analyst and psychohistorian, then sets out the epigenetic principle and the eight psychosocial stages from trust versus mistrust to integrity versus despair, each with its virtue and its typical failures. It ends with the psychopathology Erikson tied to each stage and his view of treatment, built on trust, mutuality and play. Everything here is Erikson's theory as the chapter reports it; update boxes add his later honors, Joan Erikson's ninth stage and current suicide figures.
objectives: Outline Erikson's training and career and name his main books, including the psychohistories of Luther and Gandhi.
Explain the epigenetic principle and how Erikson built on Freud's stages while adding mutual regulation with culture.
Name the eight psychosocial crises in order with their approximate ages and the virtue each can yield.
Describe the main tasks of each stage, including identity crisis, distantiation, pseudoengagement and the bond between integrity and infant trust.
Link each stage failure to the psychopathology Erikson proposed, and say why these links are hypotheses rather than proven causes.
Summarize Erikson's approach to treatment: trust and mutuality, play with children, his use of dreams and associations, and his four dimensions of the analyst's job.
